title: Gaussian Mixture Models in Hilbert Spaces via Kernel Methods
claim: Real-world data come as structured, non-Euclidean objects such as curves, graph signals and matrices that need a unified model.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, no labels, stacked-layer 3D motif
description: Three side-by-side panels with no text labels show the data types the paper handles. On the left is a line plot of several smooth hourly glucose curves in viridis colors (purple, teal, green). One bright yellow-green curve is an outlier with a large peak and dips, and faint gray curves sit in the background. In the center, a graph with gray edges is drawn across several translucent stacked planes. Its nodes are colored blue to red by intensity, which suggests signals that vary across time slices. On the right, a stack of offset heatmap layers shows correlation matrices in a red-blue diverging palette, with dark maroon diagonal-like cells. The eye goes first to the saturated heatmap and the bright yellow curve. The panels are evenly spaced and share a white background.
caption: Representative structured data samples. Left: Hourly continuous glucose monitoring paths. Center: Signals on a fixed graph with varying node intensities. Right: Correlation matrices.
abstract: Modern datasets across many disciplines increasingly consist of time-evolving, potentially infinite-dimensional random objects, such as dynamic functional data, which are naturally modeled in Hilbert spaces. In these settings, characterizing probability measures, for example, through densities, can be ill-defined or technically challenging. Motivated by clustering applications, we propose a Gaussian mixture framework for Hilbert-space-valued data based on kernel mean embeddings and develop efficient optimization algorithms for estimation. We establish theoretical guarantees showing that the proposed algorithm is well-defined and that the model yields a dense class of approximations in infinite-dimensional spaces. We evaluate the framework through extensive experiments on diverse data geometries, including $L^2$-functional data and graph signals arising in modern medical applications.
